topic_title: Why the Tip Screen Always Suggests More Than You Meant to Give

sources.title: Default Tips
sources.journal_or_venue: American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, Vol. 6, No. 3, pp. 1-19
sources.fetched_extraction: Peer-reviewed study analyzing over 13 million New York City taxicab credit-card transactions. The payment touchscreens in NYC taxis present customers with a small set of suggested tip percentages (defaults) just before payment; the specific set of defaults shown to a rider changes discontinuously at certain fare thresholds (the default menu shown for fares just below $15 differs from the menu shown for fares just above $15). Using this discontinuity in a regression discontinuity design, the authors show that the suggested default tip percentages have a large causal effect on the tip amount customers actually leave -- riders who happen to see a menu with higher suggested percentages tip more, essentially anchoring on whatever percentage the screen shows first. The paper also documents a limitation of the nudge: when the suggested defaults are set too high, a larger share of customers respond by opting out and leaving no credit-card tip at all, rather than customizing a lower amount. The study is widely cited in later research on default effects and digital tipping interfaces as the founding empirical demonstration that payment-screen tip suggestions are not neutral information but an active behavioral nudge with measurable, sizeable effects on payment behavior.

sources.title: Guilt Tipping and the Inflated Default Tip
sources.authors_or_organization: Michael Lahr, New Jersey State Policy Lab, Rutgers University
sources.journal_or_venue: New Jersey State Policy Lab (Rutgers University) policy brief
sources.fetched_extraction: Policy brief documenting the historical rise of U.S. restaurant tip norms and the mechanics of 'guilt tipping': tipping norms rose from roughly 10-15% in the early 1970s to about 20% by the late 1990s, and digital point-of-sale screens now commonly suggest tips 'as high as 35 percent of the bill.' The author argues that the shift from cash tip jars (where a tip decision was largely private) to on-screen digital prompts has made the tipping decision visible to the worker standing in front of the customer, creating direct social pressure ('guilt tipping') at the moment of choosing a percentage. The brief also cites pandemic-era data showing quick-service tip rates averaged 23.5% in April 2020, later declining to 19.8%, and notes that tips make up roughly 62% of tipped servers' income nationwide while 43 states still allow a sub-minimum cash wage for tipped workers. Overall it frames rising suggested-tip defaults as a business choice that increases revenue for the establishment with little measurable effect on customer satisfaction or repeat visits, while shifting emotional and financial pressure onto the customer at checkout.

sources.title: Fed Up Consumers Cut Tips for Restaurants, Grocery Delivery, Hotels, Taxis/Ride Services and Others, According to Popmenu's Latest Study
sources.authors_or_organization: Popmenu (consumer survey, distributed via PR Newswire)
sources.journal_or_venue: PR Newswire (press release reporting Popmenu's 2026 consumer tipping survey)
sources.fetched_extraction: 2026 U.S. consumer survey commissioned by restaurant-technology company Popmenu, published April 8, 2026. Key findings: 78% of consumers say tipping practices have 'become ridiculous'; 44% report tipping less than the previous year; 42% say they are increasingly comfortable skipping gratuities altogether. On digital tip-suggestion screens specifically, 59% of consumers say they feel compelled to leave a tip when a screen prompts them, down from 66% just seven months earlier (September 2025), and 36% now choose a custom (typically lower) amount instead of one of the preset suggested percentages, versus 32% who pick a mid-tier suggestion and 17% who pick the lowest offered option. 74% of respondents say they have noticed restaurants raising the minimum suggested tip percentage shown on digital displays. The share of pickup/counter-service orders that received any digital tip fell from 78% in 2022 to 62% in 2026, and the share of full-service diners tipping 20% or more dropped to 41%, from 45% just six months earlier. Consumers estimate they spend about $130 a year on tips they consider unnecessary, down from an estimated $150 previously. The survey frames this as a broad-based consumer pushback against the spread and escalation of on-screen tip suggestions across restaurants (35% cutting back), grocery delivery (24%), hotels (19%), and taxi/ride-hailing services (19%).
